The early Mac mini M6 also offered one of the most attractive features of this device. Although the two new Mac mini models look similar to the previous generation, Apple has removed a hidden feature that made the previous Mac mini an extremely cost-effective option.

When the M4 Mac mini was first released, it offered exceptional value for money. It not only came with Apple's M4 SoC, but also featured 16GB of unified memory, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, two front-facing USB 3, HDMI and Ethernet. At $599 original price or $499 with student discount, the M4 Mac mini was not only the most versatile Mac in Apple's lineup, but pound for pound, the best Mac in the entire series.

Video: Apple killed the best hidden feature of the Mac mini :(

However, Apple's smallest Mac had one more killer feature that made it an even better value machine: a built-in upgradeable storage slot. Users could directly pry open the back cover, unscrew a few screws, and access a removable NAND module, easily replacing it with up to 2TB of third-party SSD.

The benefits of doing so are multi-faceted. Not only can you upgrade the SSD or easily repair a damaged drive, you can also save a lot of money by not having to choose Apple's custom upgrade options and using much cheaper third-party SSDs instead.

At the time, Apple's 2TB upgrade was priced at $800, and one click of an option turned this 'budget' computer into a $1400 one. By using third-party SSDs for post-purchase upgrades, users saved close to $500.

Of course, as a DIY enthusiast, I was very excited about this and even made a full video tutorial demonstrating step-by-step how to upgrade the original SSD with a third-party drive. The video was very popular and accumulated 500,000 views.

Video: How to upgrade the SSD of the M4 Mac mini

Good times never last.

With the launch of the latest Mac mini, Apple has soldered the SSD directly to the motherboard, effectively stripping users of the ability to use third-party NAND modules for post-purchase upgrades.

The Mac mini has gone from being the undisputed king of value for money to a much more expensive one, with a price increase on top of that. Not only has the base model jumped from $600 to $900, the 2TB upgrade option has also increased from $800 to $1000.

Today, if you want to buy an M6 Mac mini with a 2TB SSD, you have to pay Apple $1900. By comparison, an M4 Mac mini of the same class with a 2TB post-purchase upgrade drive, including the roughly $320 price for the post-purchase upgrade at the time, costs about $920. Prices of course fluctuate, so a direct comparison isn't entirely possible, but this $1000 increase isn't just because Apple has raised the standard, it's because Apple has stripped users of the ability to upgrade themselves.

I can roughly guess why Apple has decided to raise the base Mac mini price by $300, and even understand why the SSD prices have been raised so much. Because of AI and other factors, prices for components, SSDs and memory have all skyrocketed. But this doesn't explain why Apple chose to solder the SSD to the motherboard instead of keeping the user-replaceable design like before.

Top liked comment by MaxM

They absolutely have the capability to do so; they just choose not to. Major markets and economies - such as the EU, China and India - need to develop strict guidelines that require smartphone manufacturers including Apple to adopt modular designs. This regulation should also extend to companies such as Sony and Microsoft. Consumer protection is basically non-existent.

We can guess, but the real reason behind Apple's decision to switch back to soldered SSDs may never be known. But what we do know is that these machines are clearly more expensive, and this statement seems to even underestimate the reality. Comparing the M4 Mac mini with a 2TB post-purchase upgrade drive to the M6 Mac mini with the 2TB custom upgrade option, it's an increase of about 106%.

9to5Mac's Take

Finding a reasonably priced base model M4 Mac mini on the second-hand market may not be easy, but if you do find one, it's still an excellent machine in terms of basic performance, features and upgradeable SSD.

One good news in this situation is that all Mac mini models come with Thunderbolt connectivity, and you can easily expand high-bandwidth external storage via USB or Thunderbolt SSDs. Personally, I'm particularly fond of the Samsung T9, which provides a relatively affordable way to add extra storage space.

Why do you think Apple decided to cancel the user-replaceable SSD design of the Mac mini? Do you have any special guesses? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
